header.title: Mort Aymeri de Narbonne (C): AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Anonymous
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's urn:geste:ed-mortaymc:dipl, from the Geste corpus of chansons de geste, Camps et al. (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.1982: The transcription adds a stray s to several line-ends (pités, loers, dotezs, lavers, garders); read through. Line 1993: . xcitezs read as .x. citez, 'ten cities'. Line 2000: Femenie, the Land of Women (the Amazons' country). Line 2002: aesmer uncertain; taken as 'tend', perhaps 'probe' or 'gauge'.
notes.3351: Line 3352: Esclabarie, a city not otherwise identified. Line 3355: Sajetaire, the Sagittaries, archer-monsters (centaurs) of romance. Line 3361: Nerbone la plus grant, 'Narbonne the great', or possibly 'the greater part of Narbonne'.
notes.1180: Line 1187: Finamonde, apparently the name of Aymeri's sword.

nodes.text: with a full twenty thousand armed knights:
I will take leave of him and of his peers,
for I am dying; it has been foretold to me
by a priest of mine who is accomplished in the arts.”
“Gladly, sire,” said Gautier the brave.
He calls for his arms; they have brought them to him;
He gives him a great blow on his gold shield,
so that he shatters it and splits open his hauberk,
and passes his spear beside his body;
at full length of his lance he throws him from the sorrel warhorse.
The devils guard him well from death,
for it does not touch him in the flesh.
When Aymeri had struck down the king,
he struck him on the helmet with Finamonde;
“Today dies the best of our kindred!”
But great pity for it has taken hold of the maidens;
the chief of them deserved high praise.
“Lords of France,” she said, “do not fear:
I will soon have healed and restored him.”
She took the count gently in her arms,
spoke three words of the Holy Trinity
and of the cross of Christendom,
at which the deadly wounds stopped bleeding;
and she has had them washed with white wine.
She draws an ointment from an ornate casket
that is worth as much as all the gold of ten cities;
with all the wealth of three crowned kings
it could not be paid for or bought.
When Jesus Christ was tormented on the cross,
when the Jews had beaten and scourged him,
the three Marys went to visit him.
Nicodemus was to keep the box;
Longinus had it carried from there to Femenie:
he loves that country because he was born there.
She has had the mortal wounds tended with it,
touched inside and dabbed outside,
and made a little of it go down his throat,
and then made him sit up and rise to his feet:
and there you see the count healed and restored.
There you would have seen great joy made.
“Lord barons,” says Hernaut the brave,
“We will go and attack the city,
Esclabarie, which stands on the ancient hill;
those who hold it are no friends of ours.
They are not pagans or Saracens,
but Sagittaries, whom may God never help;
they shoot from Turkish bows with such force
the great bolts poisoned with venom
that against their blows no armour can protect,
hauberk, helmet or mail coat.”
Aymeri has thirty ivory horns sounded;
he makes Narbonne the great resound with them,
